title: Of experience
hook: the book's last essay: know yourself through ordinary life (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was haven't you lived? It's Montaigne's answer to I've done nothing today. Your line was haven't I lived.

Some kitchens have a cook who never measures. A pinch of this, a splash of that, and somehow it comes out right. Ask for the recipe and you get a shrug: you just get a feel for it. No classroom taught that cook; ordinary dinners did. Montaigne ends his whole book with an essay built on that kind of knowing, called Of experience. Where do we really learn who we are? Not in the library, he says. In the kitchen, the sickbed, the bad temper, the night's sleep.
screen: `THE COOK WHO NEVER MEASURES.` → `A THOUSAND ORDINARY DINNERS.` → `THE LAST ESSAY: OF EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: First, where it starts. The desire to know is natural to us, Montaigne says, and we try every road to it. When reason isn't enough, we turn to experience. Then he shows how slippery reason gets: laws pile up and still can't fit every case, because life keeps producing new ones. Second, his turn inward. He studies himself, he says, more than any other subject. That is his metaphysics and his physics. It isn't a boast; he's simply the one case he can watch up close, every day. Third, what he learns. Remember how far your last anger carried you, he says, and you'll see its ugliness better than in any book of philosophy. Remember how often you were sure and wrong, and you'll trust the next certainty less. His teachers are his own illnesses, moods and mistakes, looked at honestly. Fourth, where it ends. The finest lives, he says, fit the ordinary human pattern, without miracles and without extravagance. And he closes the book not with a grand theory but with a wish for a healthy old age, borrowed from the Roman poet Horace. From the hunger to know everything, down to the plain lessons of one ordinary life: the cook's way of knowing, turned on the self.
screen: `WHEN REASON FAILS, EXPERIENCE.` · `I STUDY MYSELF.` · `REMEMBER YOUR LAST ANGER.` · `THE ORDINARY HUMAN PATTERN.` · then, large: `ORDINARY LESSONS.`

segments.voice: Bring back one small, recent moment that went a little wrong: a snapped answer, a late night that cost you the morning, a meal that sat badly. Look at it the way Montaigne looked at his own fits of temper, as a fair witness, not a judge. What did it actually teach?
Of experience. The last essay of Montaigne's book, where he says he studies himself more than anything, and learns most from the plain lessons of his own ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary lessons. The best teacher he found was the life he was already living. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: Readers often treat Of experience as the place where Montaigne's book gathers itself: he turns from theories and laws to what his own body, moods and mistakes have taught him.
